title: EXPRES: design, measured performance, and the long-baseline stability problem
reading_boundary: A selected reading path through 13 primary papers. It is not a complete bibliography of every science paper that used EXPRES.
current_status: Lowell's 2026A observer material lists EXPRES as available, including remote observing, after prior commissioning and general-use phases.
short_summary: EXPRES demonstrates that excellent short-term calibration and sub-m/s stellar residuals do not guarantee multi-year stability. Later work increasingly treats wavelength calibration, stellar line-shape change and instrument state as linked time-series problems.
latest_problem: The 2026 seven-year study found a coherent 2.8 m/s trough-to-peak drift around the 2022 temperature excursion. A regression using echellogram geometry, comb-line shapes and telemetry reduced the solar trend RMS from 1.32 to 0.43 m/s, but a deployable correction still needs era-aware validation and planet-signal preservation tests.
lessons: A calibration residual, a formal photon error and stellar time-series RMS answer different questions.
Dense laser-frequency-comb information can improve wavelength models, but the resulting change in stellar RMS can be much smaller than the calibration improvement.
Activity-correction methods can lower scatter while disagreeing on the corrected velocities; injected-signal recovery and interpretable diagnostics are therefore essential.
Simultaneous solar observations across instruments provide a practical way to distinguish astrophysical variability from instrument-specific behaviour.
Long-baseline maintenance, temperature and detector-state changes must be modelled as data eras rather than assumed stationary.

candidate_project.title: Era-aware EXPRES correction audit with planet-preservation tests
candidate_project.status: proposal for discussion, not a completed pipeline and not a statement of the EXPRES team's priorities
candidate_project.question: Can a correction learned from instrument-state diagnostics remain valid across maintenance and temperature regimes while preserving low-amplitude Keplerian signals?
candidate_project.basis: This extends the validation questions raised by the 2022 method comparison and the diagnostics demonstrated in the 2026 long-baseline study.
steps: Align science and solar RVs with laser-comb image shifts, scale and rotation, comb-line bisectors, environmental telemetry and maintenance dates.
Define instrument eras before fitting; hold out complete time blocks and at least one era rather than randomly splitting exposures.
Fit a small interpretable baseline first, then compare it with nonlinear models using the same blocked folds.
Inject Keplerian signals before correction across period, phase and semi-amplitude; report recovery bias, completeness and false positives.
Emit per-exposure state flags, correction uncertainty and an out-of-distribution warning instead of silently correcting unfamiliar states.
Reproduce the published solar and quiet-star checks before proposing any scientific use.
success_tests: Lower held-out solar and quiet-star scatter without absorbing injected Keplerian amplitude.
Stable coefficients or documented model changes across instrument eras.
No improvement claim based only on training-set RMS.
Reproducible figures and machine-readable fold assignments.
candidate_project.first_conversation: I reviewed the design, commissioning pipeline, wavelength-calibration, stellar-signal comparisons and the seven-year systematics study. I would like to test an era-held-out, injection-recovery extension of the published instrument-state correction. Before building against science products, which diagnostics can be shared and which validation case would be most useful to the team?

title: HARPS: calibration structure, instrument eras, and the 2026 hardware change
reading_boundary: Six selected technical and methods sources, not a complete bibliography of the HARPS planet surveys or all papers using archival spectra.
current_status: ESO records that HARPS returned to normal operations on 20 June 2026 after a detector, electronics, cooling and fibre upgrade; its atmospheric-dispersion corrector was then listed out of operation on 3 July.
short_summary: HARPS established the stable, fibre-fed architecture used by later precision-RV instruments. Its literature also gives a clear warning against treating a long archive as one homogeneous time series: calibration changes, the 2015 fibre exchange and the 2026 detector-era change create measurable boundaries.
latest_problem: The 2026 upgrade replaced several coupled subsystems at once. ESO has posted operational notices and a work-in-progress performance file, but the checked page says a final report will follow. Any cross-era correction should therefore be measured from standards and overlapping diagnostics rather than assumed from the earlier instrument.
lessons: Resolving power and spectrograph stability enable precise RV extraction but do not themselves define long-term accuracy.
Laser-comb tests exposed local wavelength-solution structure that a single global residual could hide.
The 2015 octagonal fibres improved illumination scrambling and throughput while introducing a star-dependent velocity offset.
Calibration solutions must be versioned on both sides of hardware changes; one offset is not automatically valid for every spectrum.
The 2026 detector, electronics, cooling and fibre work begins another measurement era whose transfer function still needs a final public characterization.

candidate_project.title: HARPS 2015-to-2026 era transfer notebook
candidate_project.status: proposal for discussion, blocked on suitable public post-upgrade standards and final performance documentation
candidate_project.question: Which observable diagnostics best predict star-dependent offsets across the 2015 and 2026 hardware boundaries without absorbing astrophysical signals?
candidate_project.basis: The 2015 fibre report measured spectral-type-dependent offsets, while the 2019 calibration paper treats the pre/post-2015 solutions separately and ESO now documents a new 2026 era.
steps: Define the hardware and pipeline eras from dated ESO notices before combining any radial velocities.
Select stable stars observed on both sides of each boundary and retain spectral type, mask, signal-to-noise and line-width information.
Estimate hierarchical offsets with star-level partial pooling and compare them with a single-offset baseline.
Hold out entire stars and time blocks; test injected low-amplitude sinusoids through the full correction.
Publish only a reproducible validation notebook and uncertainty table until the team confirms the relevant post-2026 diagnostics.
success_tests: Out-of-star and out-of-time validation improves over one global era offset.
Recovered injected amplitudes remain unbiased within their stated uncertainty.
Results change transparently when masks or spectral-type groupings change.
No post-2026 performance claim precedes the final instrument characterization.
candidate_project.first_conversation: I traced the wavelength-calibration work, the measured 2015 fibre discontinuity and the current 2026 upgrade notices. I would like to build a small cross-era validation notebook using public standards, with held-out stars and injection tests. Which post-upgrade diagnostics and stable-star set would make that comparison scientifically useful to the HARPS team?

title: ESPRESSO: on-sky precision, wavelength accuracy, and light-path validation
reading_boundary: Seven selected instrument, calibration, science and status sources. This is not a complete bibliography of ESPRESSO science programmes.
current_status: ESO lists ESPRESSO as offered, and its instrument news states that the laser frequency comb returned to full operations in November 2025 with updated performance guidance in 2026.
short_summary: ESPRESSO demonstrates sub-m/s on-sky measurements in several contexts, while its calibration literature exposes a second problem: internal sources can be precise without independently validating the entire path followed by stellar light. The temporary iodine-cell experiment turns that distinction into a practical end-to-end test.
latest_problem: The 2025 iodine-cell study reported sub-0.20 m/s end-to-end stability in its experiment but only few-m/s absolute wavelength accuracy, and found sensitivity to fibre-injection geometry. ESO separately records that laser-comb background variability affected line shapes before the comb returned to full operation. These results motivate a monitoring tool that reports precision, accuracy and illumination sensitivity separately.
lessons: The 0.10 m/s instrumental scale inferred at commissioning is not the same as every stellar time-series RMS.
Photon uncertainty, filtered short-cadence RMS and planet-model residuals answer different questions.
A dense internal calibrator can reveal structure but does not automatically validate the telescope-to-product science path.
Absolute wavelength accuracy for fundamental-constant work and differential repeatability for exoplanet RV work require different tests.
Calibration-source state and fibre-injection geometry should be explicit metadata rather than hidden pipeline assumptions.

candidate_project.title: ESPRESSO calibration-consistency monitor
candidate_project.status: proposal for discussion, not a completed pipeline and dependent on access to suitable calibration and engineering products
candidate_project.question: Can an open diagnostic compare ThAr, Fabry-Perot, laser-comb and occasional end-to-end reference measurements without confusing precision with absolute accuracy?
candidate_project.basis: The 2021 calibration comparison maps structured solution differences, the 2025 iodine experiment tests the science path, and ESO's dated notices show that calibrator state changes with time.
steps: Version every exposure by DRS, observing mode, calibrator state and fibre-injection configuration.
Compute order- and detector-position residual maps between available calibration families.
Track line-shape, background and wavelength residual summaries through time with maintenance boundaries.
Evaluate differential repeatability and absolute accuracy as separate outputs.
Hold out complete nights and hardware states; flag unfamiliar configurations rather than extrapolating silently.
Test whether any proposed correction preserves injected Doppler shifts before applying it to science targets.
success_tests: Reproduce published calibration comparisons on the same data definition.
Detect known state changes without using science outcomes as labels.
Preserve injected shifts across wavelength and illumination conditions.
Publish uncertainties and missing-metadata flags with every diagnostic.

I would like to test a small calibration-consistency monitor that keeps differential precision, absolute accuracy and illumination sensitivity as separate outputs. Which public calibration products and one validation night would make that exercise useful to the ESPRESSO team?

title: HARPS-N: wavelength solutions, solar curation, and decade-scale interpretation
reading_boundary: Six selected instrument, calibration, solar and current-status sources. It is not a complete bibliography of HARPS-N planet and atmosphere studies.
current_status: TNG's AOT54 material lists HARPS-N for normal service or visitor operation and GIARPS without restrictions.
short_summary: HARPS-N's solar programme shows why a stable spectrograph still needs evolving reduction and explicit data curation. Revised wavelength solutions improved three-year daily scatter, while the decade release identifies hardware and observing-quality boundaries and separates daily granulation from the solar magnetic cycle.
latest_problem: The decade release retains 109466 spectra after rejecting 30 percent affected by weather or understood systematics. It reports 0.49 m/s median daily RMS, 2.95 m/s raw decade RMS, and 0.41 m/s after modelling the magnetic-cycle contribution. Those values describe different selections and corrections; a reusable pipeline needs machine-readable rejection reasons and leakage tests.
lessons: A wavelength solution can change by tens of m/s locally while the combined stellar RV changes much less.
Using calibrations closer in time and selecting stable ThAr lines reduced a measurable pipeline contribution.
Rejecting weather and hardware intervals is part of the measurement definition, not clerical cleaning.
Daily solar granulation and a decade magnetic cycle occupy different timescales and require different validation.
Contemporaneous instruments provide a stronger systematics test than one instrument fitted in isolation.

candidate_project.title: HARPS-N solar quality-mask and signal-preservation audit
candidate_project.status: proposal for discussion, not a completed pipeline and dependent on the released spectra plus sufficient event metadata
candidate_project.question: Can every rejected or corrected solar interval be represented by an auditable quality flag while preserving injected rotation and planet-like signals?
candidate_project.basis: The three-year paper links improvement to wavelength recipes and calibration timing; the decade release adds explicit weather, drift, blaze and hardware curation across a much longer baseline.
steps: Encode weather, calibration-lamp, detector warm-up, drift, blaze and pipeline-version intervals as separate flags.
Reproduce the published sample counts and daily statistics from the released products.
Train no correction on the held-out year used for evaluation.
Inject sinusoids before curation across rotation and habitable-zone periods and measure attenuation.
Compare HARPS-N residuals with overlapping NEID days to separate shared solar structure from local effects.
Publish a sensitivity table showing how each flag changes cadence, RMS and recovered amplitude.
success_tests: Published counts and summary statistics reproduce within documented rounding.
Every excluded observation has a human-readable reason and source field.
Held-out signal recovery is reported alongside any RMS improvement.
Results remain traceable to raw product IDs and pipeline versions.

I would like to reproduce the quality mask as an auditable table and test how each curation step affects injected signals. title: NEID: environmental stability, illumination, solar baselines, and RV eras
reading_boundary: Seven selected subsystem, operations, solar and pipeline sources. It is not a complete bibliography of NEID exoplanet results.
current_status: WIYN describes NEID as commissioned and in full science operation; current proposal information documents the shared queue and long-term programmes.
short_summary: NEID couples sub-mK environmental control with a fibre system designed to suppress illumination errors that a wavelength reference cannot necessarily calibrate. Its public solar archive and versioned DRP records make it suitable for testing how weather, hardware events, master files and barycentric or extinction treatment propagate into RV products.
latest_problem: Current DRP documentation says the ThAr master wavelength solution has known systematics near order edges and versions etalon line lists around 2024 and 2025 changes. The 3.5-year solar release identifies 117060 usable observations, but curation alone does not show whether a correction preserves weak Doppler signals.
lessons: A 0.4 mK laboratory thermal result is not a stellar RV measurement.
Illumination changes can create errors that do not share the calibrator's optical path.
The 0.27 m/s value is a single-visit instrument requirement, not a universal achieved RMS.
Solar RMS depends visibly on sky-quality selection and time baseline.
Hardware events and master calibration files define RV eras that must accompany reduced data.

candidate_project.title: NEID RV-era and calibration-master validation notebook
candidate_project.status: proposal for discussion, not a completed pipeline and dependent on archive products and confirmed event metadata
candidate_project.question: Can a version-aware validation notebook detect order-edge and era-dependent shifts while separating weather and solar variability from instrument changes?
candidate_project.basis: The fibre paper identifies uncalibratable illumination paths, the cross-instrument study exposes a late-day trend, and DRP 1.5.2 publishes explicit wavelength-master limitations and RV eras.
steps: Join every solar and standard-star product to DRP version, RV era, wavelength master, etalon list and observing conditions.
Measure residuals by order position and barycentric velocity before pooling a scalar RV.
Test late-day or high-airmass trends against overlapping EXPRES and HARPS-N solar observations.
Hold out complete hardware eras and nights when comparing correction models.
Inject wavelength-dependent Doppler shifts and verify recovery after masking or correction.
Emit an era card and out-of-scope warning with every result.
success_tests: Known era boundaries are recovered without using planet-fit residuals as labels.
Order-edge diagnostics improve on a held-out era rather than only the training period.
Injected amplitudes remain unbiased within stated uncertainty.
Every output records data IDs, DRP and master-file versions.
